blocks.instruction: Leia o texto e escolha a alternativa correta. Algumas perguntas pedem inferência — a resposta não está escrita com todas as letras.
blocks.passage:
The rhetoric of polite disagreement is one of the most sophisticated verbal skills in British business English. It is not a trick of words; it is a small art form with rules as precise as any classical rhetoric. The senior British leader who disagrees well can change the direction of a major decision without ever sounding as if they are trying to.

The structure is usually three-part. First, acknowledgement: a specific, genuine credit to what the other side has said. Second, a gentle introduction of the alternative, framed as a question or a wondering rather than a statement. Third, an invitation to think about it together, placing the next move in the other side's hands. "I think the case for moving quickly is really strong, and I'd agree with most of what you've put forward. I suppose the question I'm left with is whether we might pay for it later in the customer relationships. Could we take ten minutes on that before we commit?"

Delivered well, this is not weakness. It is senior leadership with room for grace on both sides — and it usually wins the argument it pretends not to be having.

items.q: According to the text, the rhetoric of polite disagreement is best described as…
options: a small art form with precise rules
a sign of a weak negotiator
items.why: "it is a small art form with rules as precise as any classical rhetoric."

items.q: What are the three parts of the structure, in order?
options: Acknowledgement, gentle alternative, invitation to think together
items.why: "First, acknowledgement… Second, a gentle introduction of the alternative… Third, an invitation to think about it together."

items.q: In the sample speech, how is the alternative introduced?
options: As a wondering framed as a question
items.why: "the question I'm left with is whether we might pay for it later" — a alternativa vem como indagação, não afirmação.

items.q: The author would most likely DISAGREE with which statement?
options: Softening your language means conceding the argument.
The final move should be left in the other person's hands.
Acknowledging the other side first is part of the method.
Disagreeing gracefully can still be genuinely persuasive.
items.why: Inferência: o texto insiste que a delicadeza "is not weakness" e costuma vencer o argumento — logo, suavizar não é ceder.

items.q: The phrase "the argument it pretends not to be having" suggests that…
options: no real decision is being made
the persuasion works precisely because it does not look like confrontation
the leader is being dishonest with the room
items.why: Inferência: a força do método está em convencer sem parecer que está travando uma disputa.

blocks.instruction: Ouça Sophie orientando a nova conselheira. Responda sem ler a transcrição — ela só aparece depois de corrigir.

audio.text:
Right, so tomorrow you're going to want to push back on the chairman's plan, and my advice is: don't fight him. Not directly. In a room like that, the person who wins is almost never the one who sounds the most certain.

Start by giving him something real. Not flattery — he'll smell that in a second. Pick the one part of his case that genuinely holds up and say so, plainly. Then, and only then, raise your worry. But raise it as a wondering, not a verdict. "I suppose what I'm not yet sure about is whether the timeline leaves us any room if the regulator comes back to us." You're not telling him he's wrong. You're inviting him to look at something with you.

And here's the part people miss: hand the next move to him. "Could we take a few minutes on that before we lock it in?" You're not demanding a change; you're opening a door. Nine times out of ten, he walks through it himself, and it becomes his idea.

You keep your standing, he keeps his, and the decision quietly improves. That's the whole game.
audio.label: Ouça quantas vezes precisar. A transcrição aparece depois de corrigir.

items.q: What is Sophie's core advice about disagreeing with the chairman?
items.why: "don't fight him. Not directly."

items.q: Why does Sophie warn against flattery?
options: It wastes time in the meeting
The chairman will detect it immediately
items.why: "Not flattery — he'll smell that in a second."

items.q: How should the new board member raise her concern?
options: As a wondering, not a verdict
As a written note to the board
items.why: "raise it as a wondering, not a verdict."

items.q: What does Sophie mean by "you're opening a door"?
options: You are changing the subject entirely
You are letting the chairman arrive at the change himself
You are leaving the meeting early
You are forcing the chairman to concede
items.why: Inferência: entregar o próximo passo faz a mudança virar ideia dele — "he walks through it himself."

items.q: What does Sophie imply is the real goal of this technique?
options: To improve the decision while everyone keeps their standing
items.why: Inferência: "You keep your standing, he keeps his, and the decision quietly improves."

blocks.instruction: O vocabulário da lição aparece aqui em frases novas. Escolha o sentido ou a palavra que cabe no contexto.

items.q: "Her rhetoric was flawless — every objection sounded like an invitation." Here rhetoric means…
items.why: Rhetoric = retórica: a arte de falar de modo persuasivo (aqui em sentido elogioso).

items.q: Choose the correct word: "He opened with a genuine ___ of her analysis before raising his own doubts."
items.why: Acknowledgement = reconhecimento; creditar de forma específica o que o outro disse.

items.q: "She framed it as a wondering rather than a claim." A wondering is…
items.why: Wondering = indagação: um pensamento hesitante, colocado como pergunta, não como veredito.

items.q: Choose the correct term: "The room gave both sides room for ___, so no one had to lose face."
items.why: Grace = graça/elegância; permitir que os dois lados saiam com dignidade.

items.q: "The case for moving quickly is strong." In this business context, case means…
options: the set of reasons supporting an argument
items.why: Case (argument) = argumento: o conjunto de razões que sustentam uma posição.

blocks.instruction: Expressões e phrasal verbs que aparecem em reuniões de alto nível. Escolha o sentido no contexto.

items.q: "Two directors pushed back on the chairman's timeline." To push back on means to…
options: resist or challenge, without rejecting outright
items.why: Push back on = resistir/questionar com delicadeza, sem necessariamente rejeitar de vez.

items.q: "Nobody wanted to sign off on the plan until the risk was clearer." To sign off on means to…
items.why: Sign off on = aprovar formalmente, dar o aval final.

items.q: "Let's not lock in the decision before we've heard her concern." To lock in means to…
options: make final and hard to reverse
items.why: Lock in = fixar/fechar de forma difícil de reverter — na lição, "before we commit / lock it in".

items.q: "She raised the concern gracefully, then let the chairman come round to it himself." To come round to means to…
options: gradually accept a view one first resisted
items.why: Come round to = passar gradualmente a concordar com uma ideia que antes se resistia.

items.q: "A blunt objection rarely wins over a sceptical board." To win over means to…
items.why: Win over = conquistar o apoio de alguém — o que a discordância graciosa consegue e a rispidez não.
